description: ¡Hola! Somos EtsiBoys, un equipo de estudiantes de la Universidad de Sevilla con ganas de construir algo útil para la próxima generación de misiones lunares.
summary:
Where do you land on the Moon if you need sunlight for power and a view of Earth to talk home? Selene's Compass answers it in one screen.

Pick a site and a date. You see the real horizon around the lander, built from NASA LOLA terrain, with the true paths of the Sun and the Earth from NASA JPL Horizons on top. Countdowns tell you how long until each one sets. A calendar compares sites side by side, and a slip slider shows what you lose if the launch is delayed.

At the south pole the terrain decides everything. Our base finder starts from a permanently shadowed spot, where water ice can survive, and finds the nearest sunlit ground a rover can reach: in one case, 96% light just 1 km away.

Quickmap, Moon Trek and Horizons are powerful, but combining them takes hours. Selene's Compass turns that into seconds. It runs offline on a laptop and passes 143 automated checks.
details:
In Greek mythology Selene is the Moon, Helios is her brother the Sun, and Gaia is the Earth. That is why we called our app Selene's Compass: it tells you when Helios and Gaia can be seen from a point on Selene. For a lunar lander this is the key question, because the Sun means power and the Earth means being able to talk home.

Try it online: https://frabjous-kashata-f6eb51.netlify.app

You choose a landing site and a date and the app shows the real horizon around the lander, with the Sun and the Earth moving over it. Next to it you get the numbers that matter: how high the Sun is above the terrain, whether the Earth is visible, and how long until each one sets. For example, at Malapert Massif on 19 January 2027 the Sun will not set for 16 days, but the Earth sets in six and a half.

A calendar of days and hours, colored by whether you have Sun and Earth, Sun only, Earth only or nothing, lets you compare sites side by side. There is also a delay slider: if the launch slips one week, you can see straight away that Malapert loses contact with Earth for 9 days.

The last part is a base finder for the south pole. Water ice can survive in craters that never see the Sun, but a base there would have no power. The finder starts from one of those dark spots and looks for the closest sunlit ground that a rover could reach with a cable, keeping slopes under 15 degrees, and shows the balance between sunlight and contact with Earth. In one of our tests it found a spot with 96% sunlight only 1 km away, with a 1.4 km route.

Under the hood, the positions of the Sun and the Earth come from the NASA JPL Horizons API, computed from the lunar surface for a whole year, so libration is included. The terrain comes from NASA LOLA elevation data of the south pole. For each site we trace 720 lines around the horizon, up to 150 km away, taking the curvature of the Moon into account. Since the Moon has no atmosphere there is no refraction to correct. From this we get the percentage of time in sunlight, the longest night (which sizes the batteries), and the time windows with the Earth in view.

Everything is calculated beforehand and saved as small JSON files, so the web answers instantly and works without internet. To trust the results we wrote 143 automatic checks, for example that a site near the equator has days and nights of about 14.75 Earth days. A new light map takes around four minutes on a normal laptop.

Tools like Quickmap, Moon Trek and Horizons are very powerful, but they answer one question at a time and you need to know how to use them. Our goal was to compare sites and dates in seconds, so that a planner can react to a delay by moving a slider instead of starting a new study. It also helps anyone understand why the south pole is so difficult: there the Sun never really rises, it moves along the horizon, and a few hundred meters can change everything.

Before writing code we designed the system in Enterprise Architect: requirements, architecture and the data format shared between the calculation part and the web. Then one of us built the calculation pipeline in Python and the other built the web app in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, working in parallel thanks to that shared format. The project link is a shared folder with everything: the app ready to run, the source code, the Enterprise Architect model and a short demo video. The file 00_START_HERE explains how to open it.

Next steps. Today the app works with a list of sites we chose and checked ourselves. The next step is a point selector: click anywhere on the south pole map, or type a latitude and longitude, and the app computes that exact spot on demand. Our calculation code can already do this for any point, so the work left is connecting it to the web. After that we want to add every Artemis III candidate region and full rover routes between sites.

We used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant to help write and debug parts of the code and to draft and translate texts. All the data come from NASA sources and every result is checked by our own automatic tests.
